n: Isaac is old and nearly blind. He calls Esau, his favorite and firstborn, intending to give him the family blessing.

f.g: His physical blindness may mirror a spiritual blindness about which son should lead.

n: Isaac senses he may die soon. (He actually lives many more years—35:28.)

f.w: I know not the day of my death

n: He asks Esau to hunt game for him.
Isaac wants a favorite meal before giving the blessing. A patriarchal blessing was a solemn, prophetic act that could not be undone.

f.w: that my soul may bless thee

n: Rebekah overhears. She knows the Lord’s revelation that the elder will serve the younger (25:23), and Esau has married outside the covenant.
Rebekah tells Jacob what she overheard.
She reports Isaac’s words, adding “before the LORD”—stressing that this blessing is sacred and binding.

f.g: In the Lord’s presence; a solemn religious act.

n: Rebekah instructs Jacob to obey her plan.

f.g: Repeated in verses 13 and 43—Rebekah takes responsibility.

n: She asks for two young goats so she can cook a dish just as Isaac likes.
Jacob is to bring the meal to Isaac and receive the blessing.

f.g: The blessing carried the covenant birthright already sold to Jacob (25:33).

n: Jacob objects—not that it is wrong, but that it might fail. Esau is hairy and he is smooth-skinned.

f.g: Hebrew ḥalaq, which can also suggest “slippery” or deceitful.

n: If Isaac touches him, Jacob fears being exposed as a deceiver and getting a curse instead of a blessing.
Rebekah offers to take any curse on herself. She seems sure this course fulfills God’s word.

f.g: Rebekah accepts responsibility for the plan.

n: Jacob gets the goats, and Rebekah prepares the meal.
Rebekah dresses Jacob in Esau’s best clothes, which would carry Esau’s outdoor scent.

f.g: Fine clothing; perhaps special garments for formal occasions.

n: She covers his hands and neck with goatskins to imitate Esau’s hairiness. Later Jacob himself will be deceived with a goat (37:31-33).

f.w: the skins of the kids of the goats

n: Rebekah hands Jacob the food and bread.

f.w: into the hand of her son Jacob
f.g: The plan now depends on Jacob.

n: Jacob goes in and says, “My father.” Isaac asks, “Who are you?”—already uncertain.

f.g: Isaac’s question shows his suspicion from the start.

n: Jacob lies directly: “I am Esau your firstborn.” The deception is painful to read and later has consequences for Jacob.

f.g: Jacob’s lie is recorded honestly; he will later reap similar deception (29:25).

n: Isaac asks how he found game so quickly. Jacob even invokes God in his answer.

f.w: the LORD thy God brought it to me
f.g: Jacob brings God’s name into the deception.

n: Still unsure, Isaac asks to touch him.

f.w: whether thou be my very son Esau or not

n: Isaac feels his hands and is puzzled: the voice is Jacob’s, but the hands feel like Esau’s.

f.w: The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau
f.g: A famous line expressing a contradiction between appearance and reality.

n: Fooled by the hairy hands, Isaac begins to bless him.
Isaac asks once more, “Are you really Esau?” and Jacob says, “I am.”
Isaac eats and drinks the meal Jacob brings.
Isaac asks his son to come and kiss him.

f.g: A gesture of affection—and a final test by scent.

n: Isaac smells Esau’s clothes and is convinced. He begins the blessing, comparing his son’s scent to a field the Lord has blessed.

f.w: a field which the LORD hath blessed

n: Isaac blesses him with rain, fertile land, and abundant grain and wine—prosperity in the promised land.

f.g: In dry Canaan, dew was vital moisture for crops.

n: He blesses him to rule over nations and over his own brothers, and repeats the Abrahamic promise: those who curse him will be cursed and those who bless him blessed.

f.w: cursed be every one that curseth thee

n: Just as Jacob leaves, Esau returns from hunting. The timing is dramatic.
Esau prepares his dish and brings it in, asking for the blessing.
Isaac asks who he is, and Esau names himself—the truth revealing the deception.
Isaac trembles violently, realizing what has happened. Yet he declares that the blessing stands: “he shall be blessed.” Isaac seems to recognize God’s hand.

f.w: yea, and he shall be blessed

n: Esau cries out bitterly and begs, “Bless me too, my father!” His anguish is deeply human.
Isaac explains that Jacob came deceitfully and took the blessing.
Esau plays on Jacob’s name: he is rightly called “supplanter,” having taken both birthright and blessing. Yet Esau forgets he sold the birthright himself.

f.g: Overthrown; taken the place of by trickery (wordplay on Jacob’s name).

n: Isaac explains he has already made Jacob lord and given him the land’s abundance. What is left for Esau?
Esau pleads, “Do you have only one blessing?” and weeps aloud.

f.w: lifted up his voice, and wept

n: Isaac gives Esau a blessing too. The Hebrew can mean his home will be “of” or “away from” the earth’s richness; Edom’s land was mostly dry and rugged.

f.g: Hebrew mi-shmanne can mean “of the fatness” or “away from the fatness.”

n: Esau will live by the sword and serve his brother, but one day he will throw off his brother’s yoke. Edom was later ruled by Israel but eventually rebelled.

f.w: shalt break his yoke from off thy neck

n: Esau’s grief turns to hatred, and he plans to kill Jacob after their father dies. The Cain-and-Abel pattern threatens to repeat.

f.w: The days of mourning for my father are at hand
f.g: He plans to wait until after Isaac’s death and funeral.

f.w: then will I slay my brother Jacob

n: Rebekah learns of Esau’s plan and warns Jacob.

f.g: Consoles himself with the thought of killing you.

n: She tells Jacob to flee to her brother Laban in Haran.
She expects it to be just “a few days” until Esau calms down. In fact it will be twenty years.
She promises to send for him later, fearing to lose both sons in one day—Jacob by murder and Esau by execution or exile. Sadly, Scripture never records that she saw Jacob again.

f.w: deprived also of you both in one day
f.g: Losing both sons—one killed, the other punished as a murderer.

n: Rebekah tactfully raises another real concern with Isaac: Jacob must not marry a local Hittite woman as Esau did. This gives a covenant reason for Jacob’s journey.
